content:
Codrut Grosu prepared a nice addition to the Formal Conjectures website: allowing comments and votes. You can see a preview of this site here: https://codrut3.github.io/formal-conjectures/
For instance here you can comment on the Twin Prime conjecture and vote if you think it is a True of False statement here:
https://codrut3.github.io/formal-conjectures/theorem/?name=TwinPrimes.twin_primes

I works with github discussions: the comments and upvotes are public and associated to a github handle. This is using giscus, the same mechanism used for comments on https://leanprover-community.github.io/blog

This is a prototype, which we plan to add to to the real site soon. Any comment/vote on https://codrut3.github.io/formal-conjectures is only for testing purposes, once we enable it on the real site those discussions/voting will be permanent.

Later we also want to add easy mechanism to vote on difficulty/importance/interestingness, sorting/filtering by these votes, etc...

We welcome any feedback about this change! In particular, is the difference between liking a conjecture vs. asserting its validity clear? Do the interactive elements stand out appropriately on the page? Can you correctly guess what happens when the button is clicked based only on the icon/label?

I still think it's weird that you have 26 problems tagged as millennium prize problems when it's well known that there are only 7 millennium prize problems.

I understand why it's happening, maybe my point is that "I am a millennium prize problem" is a very well-defined thing in mathematics and "I am tagged with the millennium prize problem tag" is not the usual meaning of this.

Attempting to improve that in FC#4200: preview of that in https://mo271.github.io/formal-conjectures/ ,
This is now listing "4 files with 26 statements" for millennium prize problems on the landing page (and similar when browsing)

I think it would be good to see the docstrings of the problems in the preview.
Otherwise you really can't tell what the problem is about before first clicking on it.
That's a cool idea! I'll try and add that (this can be done in a PR disjoint to what Codrut has prepared)

The comments feature and simple voting is live:
an example:
https://google-deepmind.github.io/formal-conjectures/theorem/?name=Erdos730.erdos_730

Right now we don't support difficulty rating but you can only "like" a conjecture with a :heart: and vote for its Truth value with :thumbs_up: ("I believe this conjecture is a true statement") and :thumbs_down: ("I believe this conjecture is a false statement")

Please try it out!

It should also give an easy way to report a potential problem with a formalisation or ideas for related conjectures, etc...
Many thanks to Codrut Grosu for implementing this (and also Martin Bruse who started this work...)!

Is there a way to vote without giving this app full control over my GitHub account?

I believe I'm not the only one who would refuse approving such a thing

Good point, thanks for bringing this up. This has been a major design challenge in making this voting mechanism. We didn't want to roll our own github app (which would have been technically easier), because we rather want to use an established party solving the same problem (i.e. allowing to comment on a github issue programmatically triggered on another site)

I don't think less permission setting are possible, this is the way giscus works, perhaps one can bring this up with the giscus developers?

We specifically chose this one because it is also used at https://leanprover-community.github.io/blog/,
Could you add a link to the underlying discussion perhaps?

Snir Broshi said:

Could you add a link to the underlying discussion perhaps?

good idea. As soon as the discussion started the link is already there, top left "1 comment". But I suppose we could make it easier to find and also make sure it already appears when the discussion has not yet started..

But I guess you answered your own question: yes it is possible to vote without signing into giscus: just go the discussion page!

However, those are currently generated lazily so if the discussion hasn't started already you'd need to start the discussion in a way so that it gets picked up by giscus when rendering the website..
Perhaps we should pre-generate those discussion pages..
